summary: Describes LDP protocol extensions needed to support multi-topology routing in an MPLS environment, extending MT support from IGPs to label distribution.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7307 adds multi-topology support to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). A topology ID becomes part of each relevant prefix label binding, so separate routing maps can share one LDP session.

questions: what is an mt-id in mpls
how does ldp advertise multi-topology capability
what does invalid topology id mean in ldp
subtitle: LDP extensions that keep label bindings scoped to separate IP and IPv6 routing topologies.

tldr.problem: Multi-topology routing existed for IP, but LDP had no way to associate a prefix label with a particular topology.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7307 adds MT IP and MT IPv6 address families, includes a 16-bit MT-ID in prefix FECs and defines a capability that peers advertise before exchanging MT-specific messages.
tldr.outcome: LDP can signal label bindings for multiple topologies in one session. RFC 7307 was updated by RFC 9658.

today: RFC 7307 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2014. It has been updated by RFC 9658.

sections.title: Why LDP Needs Topology IDs
sections.content:
IP networks can use several routing topologies for different purposes. RFC 7307 extends LDP so an MPLS network can distribute labels within a selected topology. The RFC gives examples such as separating management traffic, isolating address families, using different quality-of-service profiles or assigning low-latency links to particular traffic.

The extension also defines two FEC types for LSP ping. Its central change is to make the topology part of the prefix-related forwarding-equivalence-class information used for label bindings.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can use separate routing maps for different traffic or purposes. The new topology ID tells LDP which map a label binding belongs to.

sections.title: Topology-Scoped Prefix Bindings
sections.content:
LDP assigns labels to Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs) and advertises the bindings to peers. Under this extension, a prefix-related FEC includes an MT-ID, so label binding operations take place in the context of that topology.

The MT-ID is 16 bits. MT-ID 0 represents the default topology and must be ignored when received, avoiding conflict with existing non-multi-topology procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: A label binding now includes the ID of its routing topology. ID zero represents the default topology and is ignored in this extension's procedures.

sections.title: MT IP and MT IPv6 Address Families
sections.content:
The RFC defines two address families: MT IP for IPv4 prefixes and MT IPv6 for IPv6 prefixes. Their address-family data includes a reserved field and the 16-bit MT-ID. The MT Prefix FEC element carries the prefix, its length and the topology ID.

A typed wildcard FEC can also include an MT-ID to scope an operation to one topology. The Wildcard Topology ID can be used when an operation should apply to all topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: The new address families carry an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix together with its topology ID. Wildcard operations can target one topology or all of them.

sections.title: Advertising Multi-Topology Support
sections.content:
An LDP speaker advertises a Multi-Topology capability to tell peers which address family, FEC type and topology it supports. It can advertise the capability during initialization, or later if dynamic capability announcement has been negotiated.

A speaker must not send MT FEC elements to a peer that has not advertised support. If an LSR stops supporting the capability and dynamic announcement is unavailable, it must reset the session with its peer.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers tell their peers which topologies they support before exchanging topology-specific label bindings. A router must not send those bindings to a peer that has not advertised support.

sections.title: Label Spaces, Wildcards and LSP Ping
sections.content:
Different topologies do not require separate label spaces or separate LDP sessions. An LSR can use the same label space as the default topology and signal multiple topologies in one session. The data plane cannot associate a received packet with a topology, so topology-specific label spaces cannot be used.

Typed wildcard operations can withdraw labels for one topology or use the Wildcard Topology ID to cover all topologies. The RFC also adds LSP ping sub-types for MT LDP IPv4 and IPv6 FECs. If the return path is not specified, the reply uses the default topology.
sections.plainLanguage: Topologies share an LDP session and label space. A router can withdraw labels for one map or all maps, and LSP ping can test an LSP within a selected topology.

sections.title: Errors, Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
If an LSR receives an MT-ID it does not know or support, it must discard the whole message and should send an Invalid Topology ID notification. An unassigned MT-ID also stops processing of that FEC element.

A legacy LDP node should not receive MT-related messages. Multi-topology signaling offers no specific security benefit beyond existing MPLS mechanisms; the RFC points to RFC 5036 and RFC 5920 for LDP security threats and mitigations.
sections.plainLanguage: A router rejects a message that names an unsupported topology and reports the problem. The extension depends on existing LDP security and requires peers to negotiate support.
